en: Although many think Mount Pulag is highest, Mount Apo in Mindanao is the Philippines' tallest peak at 2954 meters.
Many mistakenly believe the Pasig is the longest, but the Cagayan River in Luzon is actually the longest river at 505 kilometers.
Despite its massive size, Laguna de Bay is a freshwater lake, not a saltwater sea connected to the ocean as its name implies.
Unlike typical single cone volcanoes, Taal is a complex volcano featuring a main crater lake containing its own Volcano Island.
Contrary to the belief that the whole country shares one climate, the Philippines actually has four distinct climate types based on rainfall distribution.
Many think the Chocolate Hills are made of brown soil, but they are actually formed from marine limestone uplifted by geological tectonic forces.
Despite its nickname monkey eating eagle, the Philippine eagle primarily hunts flying lemurs and large monitor lizards in Mindanao, rarely eating monkeys.
Unlike the rest of the archipelago formed by volcanic activity, Palawan geology shows it was once part of the Asian continental shelf.
Although managed by Palawan, the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park is actually located far out in the middle of the Sulu Sea, not near the mainland.
Often mistaken for a natural wonder, the Banaue Rice Terraces are actually entirely hand carved into the mountains by the Ifugao people over 2000 years ago.
Unlike the domesticated carabao, the wild Tamaraw found in Mindoro is a distinct, smaller, V shaped species of buffalo endemic only to that island.
While often called a dormant volcano, Mount Pinatubo actually erupted violently in 1991, proving it was an active volcano rather than a permanently extinct one.
